From One-Shot to Continuous Oscillation

The previous lesson showed how the 555 timer in monostable mode fires a single timed pulse when triggered. In astable mode, there is no stable state at all — the output switches continuously between HIGH and LOW, producing a repeating waveform without any external trigger. This makes the 555 astable a simple and reliable oscillator, used in LED flashers, alarm sounders, clock pulse generators and many other applications.

The Astable Circuit

The 555 astable uses two external resistors (\(R_1\) and \(R_2\)) and one capacitor (\(C\)). The capacitor charges through both \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) in series, but discharges through only \(R_2\). This asymmetry means the time the output spends HIGH is longer than the time it spends LOW, producing a waveform where the mark time and space time are different.

The timing equations for the two half-cycles are:

  • Time HIGH (mark time): \(T_{ON} = 0.7 \times (R_1 + R_2) \times C\)
  • Time LOW (space time): \(T_{OFF} = 0.7 \times R_2 \times C\)

Period and Frequency

The total period of one complete cycle is the sum of the two half-cycles: \(T = T_{ON} + T_{OFF}\). Substituting the expressions above:

Key Fact

555 astable frequency:

$$f = \frac{1.44}{(R_1 + 2R_2) \times C}$$

where \(f\) is in hertz, \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are in ohms, and \(C\) is in farads. Note that \(R_2\) is multiplied by 2, not \(R_1\).

Period \(T = 1/f\). You can also find the period directly:

$$T = 0.7 \times (R_1 + 2R_2) \times C$$

Mark-Space Ratio

Mark-space ratio (sometimes called mark-to-space ratio) describes the shape of the output waveform:

$$\text{Mark-space ratio} = \frac{T_{ON}}{T_{OFF}} = \frac{R_1 + R_2}{R_2}$$

Because the capacitor charges through both \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) but discharges through only \(R_2\), \(T_{ON}\) is always greater than \(T_{OFF}\) when \(R_1 > 0\). This means the mark-space ratio is always greater than 1 in a standard 555 astable. A mark-space ratio of 1:1 (equal HIGH and LOW times) is called a 50% duty cycle. The standard 555 astable cannot achieve exactly 50% duty cycle unless \(R_1 = 0\) Ω (which would damage the IC), so a modified circuit using a diode is needed for a 1:1 ratio.

A 555 astable has \(R_1 = 10\) kΩ, \(R_2 = 47\) kΩ and \(C = 100\) nF. Calculate the frequency and mark-space ratio.

Step 1 — Convert units to SI base units:

\(R_1 = 10 \times 10^{3} = 10{,}000\) Ω; \(R_2 = 47 \times 10^{3} = 47{,}000\) Ω; \(C = 100 \times 10^{-9}\) F.

Step 2 — Calculate the denominator:

\(R_1 + 2R_2 = 10{,}000 + 2 \times 47{,}000 = 10{,}000 + 94{,}000 = 104{,}000\) Ω

Step 3 — Substitute into the frequency formula:

$$f = \frac{1.44}{104{,}000 \times 100 \times 10^{-9}} = \frac{1.44}{104{,}000 \times 10^{-7}} = \frac{1.44}{0.0104} \approx 138\text{ Hz}$$

Step 4 — Mark-space ratio:

$$\text{Mark-space ratio} = \frac{R_1 + R_2}{R_2} = \frac{10{,}000 + 47{,}000}{47{,}000} = \frac{57{,}000}{47{,}000} \approx 1.21$$

The output is HIGH for about 1.21 times as long as it is LOW.

Reading an Oscilloscope Trace

An oscilloscope displays voltage on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. Two key controls determine the scale: volts per division (V/div) and time per division (time/div or timebase).

To read a 555 astable output waveform from an oscilloscope trace:

  1. Amplitude: Count the number of vertical divisions from the bottom of the waveform to the top of the HIGH level. Multiply by V/div. This is the amplitude of the waveform. Do not confuse amplitude with peak-to-peak voltage — for a waveform that swings between 0 V and +9 V, the amplitude is 9 V and the peak-to-peak voltage is also 9 V (but for a waveform centred on 0 V, peak-to-peak is twice the amplitude).
  2. Period: Count the number of horizontal divisions for one complete cycle (one HIGH + one LOW). Multiply by time/div. This gives the period \(T\) in seconds (or ms or μs, depending on the timebase setting).
  3. Frequency: \(f = 1/T\). If \(T\) was measured in ms, convert to seconds before dividing: \(1\) ms \(= 10^{-3}\) s.
Key Fact

Amplitude is measured in volts (V), not milliseconds. Period is measured in time (s, ms, or μs), not volts. These unit errors are the most common mistake in oscilloscope questions. Always state the V/div and time/div values before reading off measurements.

Examiner reports identify 555 astable questions as among the worst-performing on both papers. The most frequent mistakes are:

  • Mishandling the k and μ multipliers: \(R = 47\) kΩ must be entered as \(47 \times 10^3\) or \(47{,}000\) Ω in the formula — not as \(47\).
  • Multiplying \(R_1\) by 2 instead of \(R_2\): the formula is \(R_1 + 2R_2\), so \(R_2\) gets the factor of 2, not \(R_1\).
  • Giving amplitude in ms or period in V — this is a category error. Amplitude is always in volts; period is always in time units.
  • Confusing peak-to-peak and amplitude for waveforms that swing symmetrically around 0 V.

How Diodes Control Current Direction

Diodes are two-terminal semiconductor devices that allow current to flow in one direction only. They sit at the heart of rectifier circuits and protection sub-systems, making them one of the most widely-used components in electronic design. In this lesson you will meet three roles the diode plays: passing current in a circuit, protecting inductive loads from voltage spikes, and maintaining a fixed output voltage in a regulator.

The I-V Characteristic of a Silicon Diode

A silicon diode has an anode (positive terminal) and a cathode (negative terminal). When the anode is more positive than the cathode, the diode is forward biased. Current does not flow immediately; instead, the applied voltage must overcome the forward voltage drop before significant current passes. For a silicon diode this threshold is approximately 0.7 V. Below about 0.7 V the diode conducts very little current; above this it conducts strongly. Its forward voltage varies with current and temperature.

When the anode is more negative than the cathode the diode is reverse biased. Virtually no current flows — the diode blocks it. This one-way behaviour is what makes diodes useful for rectification and protection.

Key Fact

A forward-biased silicon diode drops approximately 0.7 V across it when conducting. This value stays nearly constant over a wide range of currents — it does not increase significantly as current rises.

Protection Diodes for Inductive Loads

When a inductive load is switched off, the collapsing magnetic field induces a large reverse voltage spike. This spike can exceed the breakdown voltage of a transistor switch and destroy it in microseconds. A flyback diode (also called a freewheeling or protection diode) is connected in reverse bias across the inductive load. During normal operation the diode is reverse biased and does not conduct. When the load is switched off and the spike appears, the diode becomes forward biased and provides a low-resistance path that safely dissipates the stored energy.

A flyback diode is only needed for electromagnetic (inductive) loads: relay coils, solenoids, and motors. These devices store energy in a magnetic field.

A flyback diode is not needed for resistive loads such as lamps, heaters, or resistors. Resistors dissipate energy immediately and produce no voltage spike when switched off. A common exam error is placing a protection diode around a lamp — examiners specifically penalise this because it shows a misunderstanding of why the diode is there.

Signal path for a relay circuit with flyback protection: Supply (+) → Relay coil → Transistor collector → Transistor emitter → Supply (−). Flyback diode: cathode to the supply (+) end of the relay coil, anode to the collector end — so it is reverse biased during normal operation.

Half-Wave Rectification

Mains electricity is alternating current (AC) — the voltage repeatedly swings positive then negative. Many electronic circuits require direct current (DC). A single diode converts AC to a pulsating DC by blocking the negative half-cycles and allowing only the positive half-cycles to pass. This is called half-wave rectification.

The output of a half-wave rectifier is a series of positive pulses separated by gaps where the negative half-cycles were removed. The peak output voltage is the AC peak voltage minus the 0.7 V diode forward drop. This pulsating DC is usually smoothed by a capacitor to give a steadier supply, though smoothing is covered in a later unit.

Key Fact

In a half-wave rectifier, the diode passes the positive half-cycles and blocks the negative half-cycles. The output waveform shows repeated positive humps with gaps between them, not a continuous signal.

Zener Diodes and Voltage Regulation

A zener diode is a special type of diode that is deliberately operated in reverse breakdown. It is connected in reverse bias across the output of a power supply. When the reverse voltage reaches the zener’s breakdown voltage (also called the zener voltage, \(V_Z\)), the diode conducts in reverse and clamps the voltage at exactly \(V_Z\). Zener diodes are available in standard ratings — common values include 3.3 V, 5.1 V, 5.6 V, 6.2 V, 9.1 V, 12 V and 15 V.

How the Zener Regulator Works

The regulator circuit consists of a series resistor \(R_S\) connected between the unregulated supply \(V_{in}\) and the zener diode (cathode up to the supply, anode to 0 V). The output is taken across the zener. The series resistor drops the “spare” voltage \((V_{in} - V_Z)\) and limits the current through the zener to a safe value.

The crucial point — and the most common exam misconception — is this: if \(V_{in}\) rises, the output voltage across the zener stays at \(V_Z\). The extra voltage is absorbed by the series resistor. The zener achieves regulation by automatically increasing its conduction current to accommodate the higher input, keeping \(V_{out} = V_Z\) constant. The output does not change when the supply fluctuates — that is the entire purpose of regulation.

A 5.1 V zener diode is used to regulate a 9 V unregulated supply. The maximum zener current allowed is 40 mA. Calculate the minimum series resistance required.

Step 1 — find the voltage across the series resistor: $$V_{R_S} = V_{in} - V_Z = 9 - 5.1 = 3.9 \text{ V}$$

Step 2 — apply Ohm’s law. Use the maximum allowed current to find the minimum resistance: $$R_S = \frac{V_{R_S}}{I_{Z(max)}} = \frac{3.9}{0.040} = 97.5 \text{ }\Omega$$

The nearest standard E24 value at or above 97.5 Ω is 100 Ω, which keeps the zener current within its rating. If the question gives a zener power rating instead of a maximum current, use \(P = V_ZI_Z\) to calculate the maximum zener current.

Error 1 — adding a flyback diode to a lamp: Protection diodes are for electromagnetic loads only. A lamp is resistive; it stores no energy in a magnetic field. Adding a diode around it scores no marks and shows a conceptual error.

Error 2 — thinking \(V_{out}\) changes when \(V_{in}\) changes: The whole purpose of a zener regulator is that \(V_{out} = V_Z\) stays constant. If \(V_{in}\) increases, more current flows through \(R_S\), but \(V_{out}\) remains unchanged.

Error 3 — drawing the half-wave rectifier output incorrectly: Only positive half-cycles appear at the output. The negative half-cycles are absent (not inverted). The positive humps are separated by flat periods at 0 V, not by negative humps.

Why Symbols and Rules Matter

Before any circuit can be built or analysed, it must be drawn correctly. Examiners award marks for circuits using the correct standard symbols — a battery drawn as a single line scores no marks even if the rest of the circuit is perfect. Equally, getting the voltage and current rules wrong can cascade errors through every subsequent calculation. This lesson gives you the foundations everything else builds on.

Quantities, Units and Symbols

Three quantities appear in almost every electronics calculation. Confusing their units is the most commonly penalised error in exams.

Key Fact

Quantity — Symbol — Unit — Unit symbol:
Voltage — V — volt — V
Current — I — ampere — A
Resistance — R — ohm — Ω

Always include the unit symbol in your answer. Writing “5” when the answer is “5 V” will cost you a mark. Voltage is measured in volts (V), current in amperes (A) and resistance in ohms (Ω). These three are linked by Ohm’s law, covered in the next lesson.

Standard Circuit Symbols

Circuit diagrams use internationally agreed symbols. You are expected to know and draw the symbols for these components: cell, battery (multiple cells), resistor (rectangle), variable resistor (rectangle with an arrow), lamp, LED (arrow pointing away from the triangle), diode (triangle with a bar), capacitor (two parallel lines), switch, relay, fuse, voltmeter (circle with V), ammeter (circle with A), LDR (resistor with arrows pointing inward), thermistor (resistor with a T or slanted line), npn transistor, MOSFET, operational amplifier (triangle with + and − inputs), AND gate, OR gate, NOT gate, NAND gate and NOR gate.

Use only these standard symbols in exam circuit drawings. A rough sketch of a real component — or any invented symbol — scores zero. The specification appendix shows the exact forms required.

Series Circuits

In a series circuit, all components sit on a single loop. Two key rules apply:

  • Current is the same everywhere. If 20 mA flows through one resistor in a series chain, 20 mA flows through every other component in that chain.
  • Voltages add up. The sum of the voltages across each component equals the supply voltage: \(V_S = V_1 + V_2 + V_3\). This is a consequence of Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law.
Key Fact

Series circuit rules: current is the same at every point; voltages across each component add up to the supply voltage: \(V_S = V_1 + V_2 + \ldots\)

Parallel Circuits

In a parallel circuit, each branch connects directly between the same two points. Two rules apply:

  • Voltage is the same across every branch. A 9 V supply means 9 V appears across every parallel branch.
  • Currents add up at junctions. The total current from the supply equals the sum of the currents in all parallel branches: \(I_T = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\). This is Kirchhoff’s Current Law.

Series example: A 9 V supply drives two resistors in series. Voltmeter across R1 reads 4 V. What is the voltage across R2?

\(V_S = V_1 + V_2\) ⇒ \(9 = 4 + V_2\) ⇒ \(V_2 = 5 \text{ V}\)

Parallel example: Two branches carry 30 mA and 20 mA. What current does the supply deliver?

\(I_T = I_1 + I_2 = 30 + 20 = 50 \text{ mA}\)

Test Equipment

You need to know how to connect and use four instruments:

  • Voltmeter — always connected in parallel with the component being measured. Has very high input resistance so it draws negligible current.
  • Ammeter — always connected in series in the branch being measured. Has very low resistance so it introduces minimal voltage drop.
  • Logic probe — detects HIGH or LOW logic levels in digital circuits. It lights a different LED for logic 1 and logic 0, useful for testing gate outputs quickly.
  • Oscilloscope — displays a graph of voltage against time. The horizontal axis is time (controlled by the time-base setting, in ms/div or μs/div); the vertical axis is voltage (controlled by the Y-gain, in V/div or mV/div). Used to measure waveform amplitude, period and frequency.

A multimeter can measure voltage, current or resistance. Selecting the wrong mode — for example, connecting it in parallel on the current setting — can damage the instrument because it presents almost zero resistance across the supply.

A signal generator produces test waveforms. Three types appear in the specification:

Sine wave — a smoothly varying AC signal. The oscilloscope shows a regular S-curve. Amplitude is the peak height above zero, measured in volts from the centre line to the peak (NOT peak-to-peak).

Square wave — switches instantly between HIGH and LOW. Used to test digital circuits. Each half-period at HIGH and LOW should be equal for a 50% duty cycle.

Triangular wave — rises and falls linearly at a constant rate. Used for testing linearity of circuits.

Reading an oscilloscope: count the number of divisions for one complete cycle horizontally and multiply by the time-base value to get the period T. Frequency \(f = \frac{1}{T}\). For amplitude, count divisions from the centre to the peak and multiply by the Y-gain.

Why Combine Signals?

Many practical systems need to mix signals from several sources before amplifying them. A public address (PA) system, for example, might take input from a microphone, a keyboard and a guitar simultaneously, blend them into a single audio signal, and then boost it to drive loudspeakers. A single inverting op-amp with multiple input resistors performs this job — it is called a summing amplifier.

How a Summing Amplifier Works

The summing amplifier is an extension of the inverting amplifier. Instead of one input resistor \(R_1\), it has two or more: \(R_1, R_2, R_3\) and so on, each carrying a different input signal. All of these resistors connect to the same point — the inverting (“−”) input of the op-amp, which the negative feedback holds at virtual earth (approximately 0 V). The feedback resistor \(R_f\) still runs from the output back to the inverting input.

Because the inverting input is at virtual earth, each input resistor independently controls how much of its voltage appears in the output. The output is the inverted, weighted sum of all inputs. If all input resistors are equal (and equal to \(R_f\)), the output is simply the inverted sum of all input voltages.

Key Fact

For a summing amplifier with equal input resistors (all equal to \(R\)) and feedback resistor \(R_f\):

$$V_{OUT} = -\frac{R_f}{R} \left(V_1 + V_2 + V_3 + \ldots \right)$$

The output is the inverted, scaled sum of all inputs. The negative sign comes from the inverting input — the same phase inversion as a single inverting amplifier.

A summing amplifier can combine two or more input signals. Each input can have a different resistor value to apply a different weighting (gain) to that channel — just as a mixing desk fader adjusts how loud each instrument is in the final mix.

A summing amplifier has \(R_1 = R_2 = 10\) kΩ and \(R_f = 10\) kΩ. Two inputs are applied: \(V_1 = +0.3\) V and \(V_2 = +0.5\) V.

Step 1 — Check that all resistors are equal and equal to \(R_f\):

Since \(R_1 = R_2 = R_f = 10\) kΩ, the gain per input is \(-R_f / R_1 = -1\).

Step 2 — Calculate the output:

$$V_{OUT} = -(V_1 + V_2) = -(0.3 + 0.5) = -0.8\text{ V}$$

If instead \(R_f = 22\) kΩ (with \(R_1 = R_2 = 10\) kΩ), the gain per input becomes \(-22/10 = -2.2\):

$$V_{OUT} = -2.2 \times (0.3 + 0.5) = -2.2 \times 0.8 = -1.76\text{ V}$$

The Audio Amplifier Block Diagram

A block diagram represents a complete system as a chain of labelled rectangles. Each block is a subsystem; arrows show the direction of signal flow. The signal chain for a PA system follows a logical sequence from transducer to output.

The full signal path for a typical audio PA system looks like this:

StageBlock nameFunction
1Microphone / instrumentConverts sound to a small electrical signal (typically 1–100 mV)
2PreamplifierAmplifies the weak signal to a usable level (e.g. 100 mV to 1 V)
3Summing amplifier (mixer)Combines signals from multiple preamplified sources into one
4Power amplifierBoosts current to drive the loudspeaker
5LoudspeakerConverts the electrical signal back to sound

A common exam mistake is placing the mixer before the preamplifiers. This gives the wrong answer. The preamplifiers come first because the raw transducer signal is too weak to mix cleanly; preamplification brings each channel up to a similar level before the mixer combines them.

Key Fact

The audio amplifier chain order: Signal source → Preamplifier(s) → Summing amplifier (mixer) → Power amplifier → Loudspeaker. The summing amplifier always sits between the preamps and the power amp.

Examiners have reported that block diagram questions are among the worst answered on both papers. The most common errors are:

  • Placing the mixer (summing amplifier) before the preamplifiers — wrong because the signals are too weak to mix first.
  • Placing the power amplifier before the mixer — wrong because only one combined signal feeds the power amp.
  • Adding a block (such as a pulse generator) that has no purpose in an audio chain — read the specification carefully and only include blocks that are justified.
  • Forgetting to label each block clearly — “amplifier” alone is not sufficient if the question asks you to distinguish preamp from power amp.

Summing amplifiers appear across many practical systems beyond audio: data-acquisition circuits combine sensor readings; digital-to-analogue converters (DACs) sum binary-weighted voltages; automatic control systems blend error signals from different sensors. The key skill is recognising when multiple inputs need to be combined before the next processing stage.

Beyond the 2-Bit Counter

The 2-bit counter in the previous lesson counts from 0 to 3 in binary. Extending to more flip-flop stages gives a longer count: 3 stages count 0–7, 4 stages count 0–15. These are general binary counters. However, humans read numbers in decimal (base 10). When the count needs to be displayed as a decimal digit, a binary-coded decimal (BCD) counter is used instead. A BCD counter counts from 0000 to 1001 in binary (0 to 9 in decimal) and then resets to 0000 automatically.

The Decade Counter

A decade counter is the most common type of BCD counter. It uses 4 flip-flop stages but resets after state 9 (binary 1001), skipping states 10–15. The reset is triggered automatically by internal logic: the moment the counter reaches the forbidden state above 9, a reset pulse clears all flip-flops back to 0000.

The 4017 Johnson counter IC is specifically named in the specification. The 4017 produces ten sequential HIGH outputs (one at a time) as the clock runs, cycling through outputs Q0 to Q9 in order. It is widely used as a sequencer — for example, to light LEDs one at a time in sequence or to step a relay through ten positions. Pin 15 (MR, master reset) can be connected to a logic gate to force a reset at any desired count, creating a modulo-N counter for any N from 2 to 10.

Key Fact

The 4017 Johnson decade counter has 10 sequential output pins (Q0–Q9). On each rising clock edge, exactly one output goes HIGH and all others stay LOW. After Q9, the sequence repeats from Q0. Connecting a logic gate from a chosen Q output to the reset pin (MR) makes the counter reset early, creating a modulo-N counter for any count from 2 to 10.

Creating a Modulo-N Counter

To make the 4017 reset after counting N states (instead of 10), connect the Q\(_{N}\) output back to the reset pin (MR) via a logic gate. For example, to create a modulo-6 counter (counting 0–5 then resetting), connect Q6 to MR. When Q6 goes HIGH, it immediately resets the counter back to 0 — Q6 appears only as a very brief reset pulse and is not a usable output state.

Examiner reports show that students often miss this reset pulse and continue drawing the count sequence past the reset point. In a timing diagram, the reset causes an immediate return to 0 mid-sequence. The output that triggers the reset is a glitch — it goes HIGH and immediately LOW as the reset clears it.

Key Fact

For a 4017 with output Q\(_{N}\) wired to the reset pin (MR), the modulo is N — the counter visits states 0 through N−1 before resetting. The state at Q\(_{N}\) appears only as a fleeting glitch and does not count as a stable output.

The 7-Segment Display

A 7-segment display uses seven rectangular LED elements, labelled a through g, arranged to form the shape of a figure 8. By switching different segments on and off, the display shows decimal digits 0 to 9 and a selection of letters.

The standard segment layout (as seen from the front of the display):

PositionSegmentControls
Top horizontalaTop bar
Top-right verticalbUpper right side
Bottom-right verticalcLower right side
Bottom horizontaldBottom bar
Bottom-left verticaleLower left side
Top-left verticalfUpper left side
Middle horizontalgMiddle bar

Digit patterns for 0–9:

Digitabcdefg
01111110

Common-Cathode Displays

The specification requires knowledge of the common-cathode configuration. In a common-cathode display, all seven LED cathodes connect together to 0 V. Each segment lights up when its individual anode pin is taken to a HIGH logic level. This means a logic ‘1’ on any segment pin turns that segment ON.

The Decoder/Driver IC

A BCD counter produces a 4-bit binary output. A 7-segment display needs up to 7 individual signal lines. A decoder/driver IC sits between the two. It takes the 4-bit BCD count (inputs ABCD), converts it to the correct segment pattern for that digit, and provides enough current to light the LED segments. Without the decoder/driver, the low output current of a counter IC would be insufficient to drive the display LEDs.

As well as digits 0–9, the 7-segment display can show certain letters. The specification lists the displayable characters: A, C, E, F, H, I, L, O, P, S, U, b, d, h, n. Note that some characters use uppercase (A, C, E, F) while others use lowercase (b, d, h, n) because the display geometry cannot clearly distinguish both cases for those letters.

In an exam, you may be asked to identify the digit or letter shown by a given combination of lit segments, or to state which segments light for a given character. For the letter A: segments a, b, c, e, f, g are ON; d is OFF. For the letter C: segments a, d, e, f are ON; b, c, g are OFF.

One of the most common errors in counter questions is failing to spot a reset mid-sequence. Consider a 4017 with Q5 connected to MR. The counter counts: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and then resets to 0 immediately when it reaches 5 (because Q5 going HIGH fires the reset before Q5 can be considered a stable state).

On a timing diagram, this looks like: four complete output HIGH pulses (Q0, Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4), then a very brief glitch at Q5 as it fires the reset, then the sequence starts again from Q0. Students who do not spot the reset draw the counter continuing to Q5, Q6, Q7 — this scores zero for the sequence.

Worked rule: if Q\(_{N}\) is connected to MR, the modulo of the counter is N (not N+1). A Q5-to-MR connection makes a modulo-5 counter (states 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — five states).

Thinking in Systems

Every electronic product — from a smoke alarm to a traffic light controller — can be broken into three connected stages: an input sub-system, a processing sub-system and an output sub-system. Thinking in these three stages is one of the most powerful tools an electronics engineer has. It lets you design a complex product by solving one small section at a time.

The signal flows in one direction: from input to processing to output. Each stage has a clear role. Once you can sort components and circuits into these three categories, you can read and sketch block diagrams confidently — a skill tested on almost every past paper.

Key Fact

Every electronic system follows the same pattern: Input → Processing → Output. Input sub-systems sense the physical world. Processing sub-systems make decisions. Output sub-systems act on those decisions.

Input Sub-Systems — Sensing the World

Input sub-systems contain transducers that convert a physical quantity into an electrical signal. The specification requires you to know these sensing units:

  • Light sensor — a light-dependent resistor (LDR) whose resistance falls as light intensity increases. Used in street-light controllers and security systems.
  • Temperature sensor — an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as temperature rises. Used in fire alarms and thermostat circuits.
  • Magnetic field sensor — a reed switch that closes when a magnet is brought close. Used in door alarms and bicycle speed sensors.
  • Pressure sensor — a force-sensitive resistor whose resistance changes with applied force. Used in electronic scales and car park barriers.
  • Moisture sensor — a pair of conducting tracks whose resistance falls when wet. Used in plant-watering monitors and rain detectors.
  • Sound sensor (microphone) — a small electret microphone that converts sound pressure waves into a varying voltage. Used in clap-activated switches and intruder alarms.
  • Rotation sensor — an encoder or potentiometer that produces a voltage or pulse train proportional to angular position or speed. Used in robotic arms and motor controllers.
  • Pulse generator — an oscillator that produces a regular stream of pulses. It acts as a timing input sub-system, providing a clock signal to processing circuits such as counters and timers. It is never placed where a sensing transducer is needed — its role is timing, not physical measurement.

Processing Sub-Systems — Making Decisions

The processing stage receives electrical signals from the inputs and decides what to do. Common processing sub-systems include:

  • Logic gates — digital circuits (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR) that combine binary signals according to a truth table.
  • Latch (bistable) — a memory element that holds its output HIGH or LOW until told to change. Useful where the output must stay on after the trigger is removed.
  • Time delay — a monostable circuit that produces a single output pulse of a set length when triggered. Used in burglar alarm hold-off timers and courtesy lights.
  • Comparator — a circuit that compares two voltages and outputs HIGH when one is larger than the other. Links the analogue sensor voltage to a digital decision.
Key Fact

Processing sub-systems operate on signals — they do not interact directly with the physical world. A comparator, logic gate, latch or timer all sit in the processing stage, never in the input or output stage.

Output Sub-Systems — Acting on Decisions

Output sub-systems convert the processed electrical signal back into something physically useful. The specification lists these output devices:

  • Lamp / LED — visual indicators. LEDs require a current-limiting resistor in series.
  • Buzzer — an audio output. Some are “active” (buzzes at a fixed frequency when supplied with DC); others are “passive” (require an AC or pulsed signal).
  • Solenoid — an electromagnetic coil that produces linear motion when energised. Used to release door locks or trigger valves.
  • Motor — converts electrical energy into continuous rotation. Used in fans, conveyor belts and robots.
  • Servo — a geared motor with a position feedback circuit, allowing controlled angular movement. Used in robotic arms and model aircraft control surfaces.
  • Loudspeaker — a high-power audio output that requires an amplifier stage between the processing circuit and the speaker coil.

Most output devices cannot be driven directly by a logic gate or comparator because they need more current than those circuits can supply. A transducer driver — typically a transistor or MOSFET switch — sits between the processing output and the device to boost current capacity.

A security light turns on when it is dark AND someone is moving nearby. Break this into three stages:

Input: Two sensors are needed — an LDR (detects darkness) and a PIR motion sensor (detects movement). Each is an input sub-system.

Processing: The light should only come on if it is dark AND movement is detected. An AND logic gate combines the two signals: output is HIGH only when both inputs are HIGH.

Output: The lamp (output device). Because the AND gate cannot supply enough current to drive the lamp directly, a transistor switch (transducer driver) is added between the gate output and the lamp.

Block diagram: The LDR sensor and PIR sensor both feed the AND gate. The AND gate feeds the transistor driver, which feeds the lamp.

Examiners have consistently penalised three types of error in block diagrams:

1. Mixing up stages. Putting a logic gate in the input stage or a thermistor in the output stage. Remember: transducers are always inputs; decision circuits are always processing; actuators are always outputs.

2. Inventing blocks not needed by the specification. Adding a pulse generator where no timing is required (e.g. a simple light sensor to LED circuit needs no clock). Only include a block if the system description justifies it.

3. Omitting the transducer driver. When the output is a motor, relay, solenoid or lamp, a transistor or MOSFET driver is almost always required. Logic gates and comparators cannot supply the current these devices need directly.

From Sensor to Signal

A resistive sensor on its own produces a change in resistance, not a change in voltage. To turn a varying resistance into a varying voltage that a comparator or logic gate can read, you use a voltage divider. This is the most common input circuit in electronics and it appears on virtually every exam paper.

How a Voltage Divider Works

Two resistors, R1 and R2, are placed in series across a supply voltage \(V_{in}\). The output voltage \(V_{out}\) is taken from the junction between them and is given by:

$$V_{out} = V_{in} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$

If R2 is much larger than R1, most of the supply voltage appears across R2, so \(V_{out}\) is high. If R2 is much smaller than R1, most of the voltage is dropped across R1 and \(V_{out}\) is low. Replacing one of the resistors with a sensor (LDR, thermistor, etc.) makes \(V_{out}\) change with the physical quantity being sensed.

Key Fact

Voltage divider: \(V_{out} = V_{in} \times \dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\). \(V_{out}\) is taken across R2. If R2 increases relative to R1, \(V_{out}\) increases. If R2 decreases, \(V_{out}\) decreases.

LDR Sensing Circuit — Light Level Detection

A light-dependent resistor (LDR) has a high resistance in the dark (hundreds of kilohms) and a low resistance in bright light (hundreds of ohms). In a voltage divider with the LDR as R1 and a fixed resistor as R2:

  • In the dark: LDR (R1) is large ⇒ most voltage drops across R1 ⇒ \(V_{out}\) is LOW.
  • In bright light: LDR (R1) falls ⇒ less voltage drops across R1 ⇒ \(V_{out}\) rises towards \(V_{in}\).

Swapping the positions of the LDR and the fixed resistor (putting the LDR as R2 instead of R1) reverses the behaviour: \(V_{out}\) is HIGH in the dark and LOW in the light. The examiner has penalised this error repeatedly — always identify which resistor is connected to 0 V to determine what happens to \(V_{out}\).

NTC Thermistor Sensing Circuit — Temperature Detection

An NTC thermistor works on the same principle. Its resistance falls as temperature rises. In a divider with the thermistor as R1:

  • Cold: thermistor resistance is high ⇒ large voltage drop across thermistor ⇒ \(V_{out}\) is LOW.
  • Hot: thermistor resistance falls ⇒ smaller voltage drop across thermistor ⇒ \(V_{out}\) rises.

If the circuit needs to trigger when it gets cold (e.g. a frost alarm), place the thermistor as R2 so \(V_{out}\) rises as temperature falls. This “orientation” decision is the main skill tested on exam questions about sensing circuits.

Key Fact

Sensor orientation determines output behaviour. Sensor as R1 (top): \(V_{out}\) rises when sensor resistance falls (e.g. hotter, brighter). Sensor as R2 (bottom): \(V_{out}\) falls when sensor resistance falls. Getting this wrong produces the opposite output to what is wanted.

Other Sensing Types

The same voltage-divider principle applies to all resistive sensors in the specification:

  • Pressure sensor (force-sensitive resistor): resistance decreases under applied force. Used in electronic door mats and scales.
  • Moisture sensor: two copper tracks on a PCB; resistance falls when water bridges the gap between them. Used in plant-watering monitors.
  • Sound sensor (electret microphone + amplifier): produces a small AC voltage proportional to sound level. The signal is amplified before being fed into a comparator.
  • Potentiometer (variable resistor): a manually-adjusted voltage divider. The wiper provides a continuously variable \(V_{out}\) between 0 V and \(V_{in}\).

Pulse Generator as an Input Sub-System

A pulse generator produces a regular square wave. It is used as a timing input — for example, providing the clock pulses that advance a counter. The output of the pulse generator feeds the clock input of a processing circuit; it is never placed in the sensor position of a voltage divider.

Pull-up and pull-down resistors are used with switches and other two-state inputs to ensure the logic level is well-defined when the switch is open. A pull-up resistor (connected between the input pin and the positive supply) holds the logic level HIGH when the switch is open; the switch itself pulls it LOW when closed. A pull-down resistor does the reverse.

Sizing the LED Current-Limiting Resistor

When an LED is included in a sensing circuit output, a series resistor limits the current to a safe value. The LED has a typical forward voltage (given in the exam data: approximately 2 V for a red LED, 3 V for blue or white). The resistor takes the remaining voltage:

$$R = \frac{V_{supply} - V_{LED}}{I_{LED}}$$

For a 9 V supply, a 2 V red LED and a target current of 10 mA: \(R = (9 - 2)/0.010 = 700 \text{ }\Omega\). The nearest E24 value above 700 Ω is 750 Ω — always round up to keep current at or below the target.

Problem: A 9 V supply, a 10 kΩ fixed resistor (R1, top) and an LDR (R2, bottom). In daylight, the LDR resistance is 1 kΩ. Calculate \(V_{out}\).

\(V_{out} = V_{in} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = 9 \times \frac{1000}{10000 + 1000} = 9 \times \frac{1000}{11000} = 9 \times 0.0909 = 0.82 \text{ V}\)

This LOW output voltage would not trigger a HIGH logic level. If the circuit is supposed to activate in daylight, the positions of R1 and R2 should be swapped.

The most common mistake in sensing circuit questions is drawing the resistor and sensor in the wrong order. A question might ask for a circuit that triggers when it is warm. If you place the thermistor as R1 (top) and the fixed resistor as R2 (bottom), \(V_{out}\) rises when the thermistor gets hot — that’s correct. If you accidentally swap them, \(V_{out}\) falls when it gets hot, which is the opposite of what is required.

Always write a one-line logic check before drawing: “Hot ⇒ thermistor resistance falls ⇒ if thermistor is R1, \(V_{out}\) rises ⇒ correct for triggering on warmth.” This takes five seconds and prevents the most penalised error in sensing circuit questions.

From Problem Statement to Logic Circuit

Logic design starts with a written specification — a statement describing exactly when the output should be Logic 1. Your job is to translate that statement into a truth table, extract a Boolean expression, and select the gates to build it. This three-step pipeline is tested in nearly every exam paper and is the foundation of all digital design work.

Once you can design with standard gates, you will learn the most important conversion skill in this unit: replacing every gate in a circuit with NAND-only implementation. This matters because NAND gates are universal — any logic function can be built from them. In practice, a designer who needs only one type of IC can buy a single 4-NAND chip (such as the CMOS 4011) and implement any function without stocking multiple gate types.

Step 1 — Design from a Specification

Consider a burglar alarm that should activate (output = 1) when the door sensor (A) is 1 and the motion sensor (B) is 1, or when the panic button (C) is pressed (1). The Boolean expression is \(Q = A \cdot B + C\). The truth table has 8 rows (three inputs, \(2^3 = 8\) combinations). Rows where A=1 and B=1, or C=1, give Q=1.

The gate realisation needs an AND gate (inputs A and B) feeding into an OR gate alongside input C. This is a standard sum of products form. Most combinational logic specifications can be written as a sum of products, making the gate selection straightforward.

Key Fact

The three steps for logic design: (1) write the truth table from the specification; (2) write the Boolean expression from the rows where Q=1; (3) select the gates that match the expression. Every logic design question on the exam follows this pipeline.

NAND Equivalents for Each Gate

The conversion to NAND-only is systematic. There is a known NAND equivalent for every standard gate. Learn these four equivalents and the conversion becomes mechanical:

NAND equivalents for standard logic gates
Standard gateNAND-only equivalentBoolean check
NOT (A) One NAND gate with both inputs tied to A \(\overline{A \cdot A} = \overline{A}\)
AND (A, B) One NAND followed by a tied-input NOT-NAND on its output \(\overline{\overline{A \cdot B}} = A \cdot B\)
OR (A, B) NOT-NAND each input separately, then combine with a third NAND \(\overline{\overline{A} \cdot \overline{B}} = A + B\)
NOR (A, B) OR-equivalent (three NANDs) followed by a tied-input NOT-NAND \(\overline{A + B}\)
Key Fact

The three most important NAND equivalents: NOT = one NAND with inputs tied together; AND = NAND followed by a tied-input NAND on its output; OR = NOT-NAND each input separately, then combine with a third NAND.

The Conversion Algorithm — Three Steps

When the exam asks you to convert a circuit to NAND only, follow this exact sequence:

Step 1 — Redraw with NAND equivalents. Replace each gate in the original circuit with its NAND equivalent from the table above. The intermediate circuit will now contain only NAND gates — but it may have more gates than necessary.

Step 2 — Identify back-to-back (double inversion) pairs. Scan the circuit for any point where a NAND output connects directly into the “both-inputs-tied” (NOT-configured) NAND input. Two inversions in a row cancel out: \(\overline{\overline{X}} = X\). Mark these pairs.

Step 3 — Cancel the back-to-back pairs. Remove both back-to-back NANDs and connect the wire directly. This simplifies the circuit and reduces gate count. The resulting circuit is the minimal NAND-only implementation.

Original circuit: AND gate (inputs A, B) feeding an OR gate alongside input C. Boolean: \(Q = AB + C\).

Step 1 — Replace the AND gate with NAND(A,B) followed by a tied-input NAND on its output. Replace the OR gate with a NOT-NAND on each of its inputs, then combine those outputs with a third NAND. Intermediate circuit has 5 NAND gates.

Step 2 — The output of the tied-input NAND after the AND gate feeds directly into the tied-input NAND on the OR-equivalent side. These two are back-to-back — double inversion identified.

Step 3 — Cancel: remove those two back-to-back NANDs and connect the NAND(A,B) output directly to the input of the final NAND. Final circuit uses 3 NAND gates: NAND(A,B), NOT-NAND(C,C), NAND of those two results. Boolean check: \(\overline{\overline{AB} \cdot \overline{C}} = AB + C\) — correct by De Morgan.

Double Inversion and De Morgan’s Theorem

Double inversion is the key simplification step. Any time a signal passes through two inverters in a row (or two tied-input NANDs), both can be removed. This is the step that students most commonly miss in the exam — they draw a correct but bloated NAND circuit with redundant gate pairs still in place.

De Morgan’s theorem states \(\overline{A} \cdot \overline{B} = \overline{A + B}\), which rearranges to show that NAND of the complements equals the OR, and \(\overline{\overline{A} \cdot \overline{B}} = A + B\), confirming the OR equivalent. You do not need to prove De Morgan in the exam — apply it to verify your NAND conversion is correct.

Logic ICs: The CMOS 4000 Series

In practice, logic gates are packaged as CMOS 4000 series ICs. Each IC package contains several identical gates sharing a power supply pin (VDD) and a ground pin (VSS). The 4011 contains four two-input NAND gates; the 4001 contains four two-input NOR gates. When using these ICs, unused inputs must be tied to Logic 0 or Logic 1 (not left floating) to prevent unpredictable switching.

A 14-pin dual in-line (DIL) package has 7 pins on each side. The notch or dot marks pin 1 (top left). Pins are numbered anticlockwise from pin 1. For a quad 2-input NAND (4011): pin 14 is VDD (supply), pin 7 is VSS (ground). The four gates share these supply pins — you only need to connect VDD and VSS once for all four gates.

In exam questions showing a pinout, identify the gate inputs and outputs by their pin numbers. A question might ask you to state which pins to connect to implement a specific logic function using available gates on the IC. Always check that you are using a gate that is on the IC — examiners have penalised students who used the wrong gate type for the IC shown.

Switching High Currents from Low-Power Signals

A logic gate or comparator output can drive only a few milliamperes — not nearly enough to light a lamp, spin a motor or click a relay. A transistor or MOSFET acts as a current amplifier and electronic switch, letting a small control signal turn a much larger load current on or off. Examiners report this is poorly understood every year, so this lesson builds the skill in both directions: forward (given a signal, will the device switch?) and backward (given a required load current, what control signal do I need?).

The npn Bipolar Transistor as a Switch

An npn transistor has three terminals: base (B), collector (C) and emitter (E). In a switching circuit:

  • The load (lamp, relay coil, etc.) is connected between the positive supply and the collector.
  • The emitter connects to 0 V (ground).
  • A base resistor connects the control signal to the base, limiting the base current to a safe value.

The transistor turns on (saturates) when a sufficient base current flows. The base-emitter voltage \(V_{BE}\) is approximately 0.7 V when the transistor is on. Any control voltage above about 0.7 V (after the base resistor voltage drop) will start to turn the transistor on. To ensure full saturation, the base current \(I_B\) must be at least \(I_C / h_{FE}\), where \(I_C\) is the required collector (load) current and \(h_{FE}\) is the transistor’s DC current gain from its data sheet.

$$I_B = \frac{I_C}{h_{FE}}$$

Key Fact

npn transistor switch: \(V_{BE} \approx 0.7 \text{ V}\) when on. Current gain \(h_{FE} = I_C / I_B\). To saturate the transistor: \(I_B \geq I_C / h_{FE}\).

Problem: A transistor with \(h_{FE}\) = 100 must switch a lamp drawing 200 mA. The control signal is 5 V. Find the minimum base current needed and a suitable base resistor value.

Step 1 — minimum base current: \(I_B = I_C / h_{FE} = 200 / 100 = 2 \text{ mA} = 0.002 \text{ A}\)

Step 2 — voltage across base resistor: \(V_{RB} = V_{IN} - V_{BE} = 5 - 0.7 = 4.3 \text{ V}\)

Step 3 — base resistor: \(R_B = V_{RB} / I_B = 4.3 / 0.002 = 2150 \text{ }\Omega\). Nearest E24 value below 2150 Ω is 2.0 kΩ. This gives \(I_B = 4.3/2000 = 2.15 \text{ mA}\), which meets the minimum.

The n-Channel Enhancement-Mode MOSFET

An n-channel MOSFET has three terminals: gate (G), drain (D) and source (S). Unlike the bipolar transistor, the MOSFET is voltage-controlled: almost no gate current flows, so the control circuit does not need to supply base current. This makes MOSFETs ideal for driving high-power loads.

The MOSFET turns on when the gate-to-source voltage \(V_{GS}\) exceeds the threshold voltage \(V_{GS(th)}\). For calculations, the threshold is taken as 3 V. When fully on (in the linear region), the drain current \(I_D\) is controlled by the transconductance:

$$I_D = g_m (V_{GS} - V_{GS(th)})$$

where \(g_m\) is the transconductance in siemens (S or A/V). In a typical exam question \(g_m\) is given; you substitute \(V_{GS}\) and \(V_{GS(th)} = 3 \text{ V}\) to find \(I_D\).

Key Fact

MOSFET: \(I_D = g_m(V_{GS} - V_{GS(th)})\). Threshold \(V_{GS(th)} = 3 \text{ V}\) (assumed). Gate current = 0. Turns on when \(V_{GS} > 3 \text{ V}\).

Problem: An n-channel MOSFET has \(g_m = 0.5 \text{ S}\) and \(V_{GS(th)} = 3 \text{ V}\). The gate voltage is 7 V. Calculate the drain current.

\(I_D = g_m(V_{GS} - V_{GS(th)}) = 0.5 \times (7 - 3) = 0.5 \times 4 = 2 \text{ A}\)

This 2 A drain current could drive a motor. A bipolar transistor base circuit would need \(I_B = 2/h_{FE}\) — at \(h_{FE}\) = 100, that’s 20 mA just to bias the base, which overloads a logic gate output. The MOSFET avoids this entirely because its gate draws negligible current.

Choosing between npn and MOSFET

Use an npn bipolar transistor for low-to-medium current loads (up to around 100–200 mA) where the control circuit can supply a few milliamps of base current. Use an n-channel MOSFET for high-current loads (motors, solenoids) or where the control source (such as a logic gate output) cannot supply even a small base current. Both are placed between the processing sub-system and the output device as a transducer driver.

Electromagnetic loads (relays, solenoids, motors) need a protection diode connected in reverse bias across the load. When the transistor or MOSFET switches off, the coil’s collapsing magnetic field generates a large voltage spike (back-EMF) that can destroy the switch device. The diode clamps this spike. Note: a protection diode is only needed for electromagnetic loads, not for resistive loads like lamps.

From Analogue World to Digital Logic

Real-world signals are messy. A temperature sensor produces a voltage that drifts slowly; a mechanical switch bounces several times before settling; a radio receiver picks up interference alongside the wanted signal. Logic gates, however, demand a clear HIGH or LOW — nothing in between. Schmitt inverter circuits sit at the boundary between the analogue world and the digital one, converting uncertain voltages into clean, decisive logic levels.

What Is a Schmitt Trigger?

A standard logic inverter switches output the moment its input crosses one fixed voltage threshold — roughly half the supply. Any noise near that threshold causes the output to flicker rapidly between HIGH and LOW. A Schmitt trigger solves this by using two separate thresholds:

  • The upper threshold voltage (VT+) — the input must rise above this level to switch the output LOW (since it is an inverter).
  • The lower threshold voltage (VT−) — the input must fall below this level to switch the output HIGH.

The gap between the two thresholds is called hysteresis. Noise that does not carry the input across the next switching threshold cannot change the output. The output only changes when the input makes a definitive excursion past one of the thresholds.

Key Fact

A Schmitt inverter has two thresholds: it switches LOW when Vin rises above VT+ and switches HIGH when Vin falls below VT−. The difference (VT+ − VT−) is called hysteresis, and it acts as a noise immunity band.

Reading Thresholds from a Graph

Exam questions frequently show a voltage–time graph of the input signal alongside the output waveform and ask you to identify the threshold voltages. Follow these steps carefully:

  1. Use a ruler — line it up horizontally with the input voltage at the exact moment the output changes state.
  2. Read the voltage on the y-axis against that horizontal line. Do this for each transition: one reading when the output goes LOW (this is VT+) and one when it goes HIGH (this is VT−).
  3. Check that VT+ is always greater than VT−. If your reading gives VT− > VT+, you have swapped them — re-read the graph.

Suppose a graph shows an input voltage rising slowly from 0 V. The output (initially HIGH) suddenly switches LOW when the input reaches 3.5 V. Later, the input falls back down and the output switches HIGH again when the input passes 1.5 V.

From these observations: VT+ = 3.5 V and VT− = 1.5 V. Hysteresis = 3.5 − 1.5 = 2.0 V. A noise spike changes the output only if it carries the input across the relevant switching threshold.

Switch Debouncing

When you press a mechanical switch, the metal contacts do not simply close once — they bounce apart and make contact again several times in the first millisecond. To a digital circuit running at millions of cycles per second, those bounces look like many separate button presses. This is called contact bounce. It causes counting circuits to register extra counts and microcontrollers to trigger multiple times from a single press.

A Schmitt inverter fixes this problem. The output only changes state when the input voltage crosses a threshold by a margin larger than the hysteresis band. Because the bounce amplitude is typically small, the input flickers around one threshold level without cleanly crossing the other one. The result: one clean output transition for each deliberate press of the switch.

Key Fact

Switch debouncing is one of the most common uses for a Schmitt inverter. The hysteresis band filters out the small-amplitude contact-bounce pulses, so the logic circuit downstream sees only one clean HIGH-to-LOW (or LOW-to-HIGH) transition per press.

Comparing Three Analogue-to-Digital Interface Methods

There are three circuit methods for converting a slowly-changing analogue signal (such as from a sensor) into a digital logic signal. The specification requires you to compare them:

Method How it works Key advantage Key limitation
Transistor switch Base voltage exceeds ~0.7 V → transistor saturates → output goes LOW Simple; drives a load directly Single threshold; susceptible to noise at the switching point
Op-amp comparator V+ > V− → output HIGH; V+ < V− → output LOW; threshold set by a voltage-divider reference on one input Precise, adjustable threshold; fast response Single threshold; output can chatter near the crossover if input is noisy
Schmitt inverter Dual thresholds (VT+ and VT−); output only changes when input crosses one threshold heading away from the other Noise immunity from hysteresis; clean output even with noisy or slow-changing inputs Thresholds are fixed by the chip; less adjustable than a comparator with a reference

Confusing which threshold triggers which transition. Remember the Schmitt is an inverter: a HIGH input gives a LOW output. So when Vin rises above VT+, the output goes LOW — not HIGH. Sketch the logic truth and check your graph reading makes sense with this inversion.

Missing the ruler. Examiner reports consistently note that students lose marks by estimating threshold voltages by eye rather than aligning a ruler precisely with the graph gridlines. Use the grid squares as guides and always read off where the output actually changes, not where it looks like it should.

Swapping the hysteresis direction. Hysteresis is always VT+ minus VT−, a positive number. If your answer gives a negative hysteresis, you have the thresholds swapped.

Slow-Changing Signals and Noise Rejection

A thermostat sensor or a light-dependent resistor in a dimming-light circuit produces voltages that drift slowly. If that signal is fed directly into a standard logic gate, any small ripple on the supply or interference from a nearby radio can push the input just over the threshold — triggering a false output. The Schmitt inverter is the natural choice in these situations: its output stays locked until the input has moved decisively through the full hysteresis window, ignoring incidental noise along the way.

This makes the Schmitt inverter the preferred building block wherever a sensor signal transitions slowly from one state to another — light sensors moving from dark to bright, temperature sensors crossing a set-point, or any signal that takes milliseconds or longer to change level. The transistor switch and comparator methods, while useful, require additional filtering components to achieve the same noise immunity that the Schmitt trigger delivers with no extra parts.

Storing a Single Bit

Logic gates process information instantly — their output changes as soon as their inputs change. But digital systems also need to store information: a counter must remember its current count between clock pulses, and a memory circuit must hold data after the input is removed. The simplest storage element in digital electronics is the D-type flip-flop.

The D-Type Flip-Flop

A D-type flip-flop has three inputs — D (data), CLK (clock) — and two complementary outputs, Q and \(\overline{Q}\) (Q-bar). The key property is that it is rising-edge triggered: the flip-flop samples the D input only at the instant the clock signal transitions from LOW to HIGH. At all other times, changes on D have no effect.

Key Fact

At every rising clock edge: Q copies the value of D. Between rising edges: Q holds its stored value regardless of what D does. \(\overline{Q}\) is always the logical opposite of Q.

In symbol form, the D-type is drawn as a rectangle with D and CLK on the left, Q on the right, and \(\overline{Q}\) on the right with a small circle (bubble) to indicate inversion. The clock input is marked with a small triangle to indicate edge-triggering.

Timing Diagram for a D-Type Flip-Flop

A timing diagram shows the D, CLK, Q and \(\overline{Q}\) signals plotted against time. Reading one systematically is a core exam skill.

Consider the following sequence (read each rising clock edge left to right):

Rising edgeD at that momentQ after edgeQ-bar after edge
1st110
2nd001
3rd001
4th110

Between any two consecutive rising edges, Q stays constant — even if D changes. This is the “latch” behaviour: the flip-flop has stored the bit from the previous rising edge and holds it until the next one.

The D-Type as a Data Latch

When a D-type flip-flop is used to hold a data bit so it can be read later, it is described as a data latch. The flip-flop “latches on” to the value of D at the rising clock edge and holds it. This is useful when a sensor produces a brief pulse that would otherwise be lost before a processor can act on it.

Binary Counters from D-Type Flip-Flops

If the \(\overline{Q}\) output of a D-type flip-flop is connected back to its own D input, the circuit divides the input clock frequency by 2. Each rising clock edge causes the flip-flop to toggle — the output alternates between 0 and 1 every clock cycle. This is a 1-bit binary up-counter.

Key Fact

To make a 1-bit binary counter: connect \(\overline{Q}\) back to D. Each rising clock edge causes Q to toggle. The output at Q has half the frequency of the clock input.

The 2-Bit Counter

Two D-type flip-flops connected in series form a 2-bit counter. The Q-bar output of the first flip-flop (Q0) clocks the second flip-flop. Both flip-flops have their \(\overline{Q}\) connected back to their own D input.

The result: Q0 toggles on every rising edge of the external clock (CLK). Q1 toggles when Q0 falls, which is the rising edge of Q-bar. So:

Clock countQ1Q0Binary value
0000
1011
2102
3113
4000 (reset)

The counter cycles through 0, 1, 2, 3, then resets to 0 — a modulo-4 count. This is a 2-bit binary up-counter. Q0 is the least significant bit (LSB); Q1 is the most significant bit (MSB).

A clock with a frequency of 4 Hz feeds a 2-bit counter made from two D-type flip-flops.

First flip-flop (Q0): toggles at every rising clock edge. Frequency of Q0 = \(4 / 2 = 2\) Hz.

Second flip-flop (Q1): toggles at every rising edge of Q0. Frequency of Q1 = \(2 / 2 = 1\) Hz.

The pattern: each stage divides the previous frequency by 2. If Q0 is connected to an LED, that LED flashes at 2 Hz. If Q1 is connected to an LED, it flashes at 1 Hz — half the rate of Q0’s LED. This frequency-halving at each stage is the key fact examiners test.

If the exam asks for the expected frequency of Q0 and Q1 from a 12 Hz clock:
Q0 = 12 / 2 = 6 Hz
Q1 = 6 / 2 = 3 Hz

A 2-bit counter timing diagram shows four waveforms stacked vertically: CLK (external clock), Q0 (fastest, half CLK frequency), Q1 (slowest, half Q0 frequency).

CLK: a square wave toggling continuously. Q0: toggles at each rising edge of CLK — its period is twice that of CLK. Q1: toggles when Q0 falls, which is the rising edge of Q-bar — its period is twice that of Q0 (four times CLK).

To check: count CLK pulses between rising edges of Q1. There should be exactly 4 CLK pulses per Q1 cycle. If you see 4, you have drawn the diagram correctly. Common error: drawing Q1 toggling on Q0’s rising edge instead of its falling edge.
